The opening just might be my favourite opening ever.

An interesting thing in the opening is that the near the end of the OP the MC's little sister runs down the same path that Nao and Yuu went to when they went outside with Nao's brother. I hope that that's just some reused assets and not some foreshadowing, but Yuu's ability is the one a government would be most interested in...

Knowing Jun Maeda, there's going to be a lot more suffering than just in this episode. I would be shocked if Charlotte's brother is the only one who gets a taste.

We've gotten some pretty heavy indication that Charlotte is a little damaged personality wise. She quite obviously has two modes of behavior. She's got her aloof cool attitude which is definitely a coping mechanism and her normal cheerful attitude which has slipped out a few times and was very visible in the flashbacks.

I expect tears.
But we already had tears this episode, with Comrade-kun! At least I think those were tears. He might just be naturally moist.

I think the theory of powers having something to do with teen trauma has been bolstered, and gets a bit of a boost though not a substantial one.

  1. In Nao's case, her invisibility could be directly related to her inability to trust others and her circumstance of hiding from "the scientists." As for it only affecting one person, well, it would seem that all of the powers are fairly nerfed in some way, so it must be limited on that front. However, this raises the question as to what would cause her powers to demanifest - probably coming to trust others (no more reason to hide).
  2. In Thoughtography's case, target shooters - be it shooting guns or shooting freethrows in basketball - often make use of visualization. That an archer would be able to manifest this ability as a superpower would make sense - however, in this guy's case, it would seem that the catalyst for power formation isn't necessarily the same thing as what creates the power. Hypothetically, his power might disappear once he finds a more responsible way to deal with the catalyzing financial problems.
  3. In Nao's brother's case, we also learn that power-formation can be catalyzed by some trauma (financial problems) but then manifested in a positive personality attribute, such as a passion for music. Even though the power is related to something they like, it also has the same wear-off reason as any others - when you're a teen, the passions you have at one point don't always persist. Dreams of being a rockstar are surprisingly short-lived. Also, the whole torture thing probably didn't help, either.

The episode's ending left me somewhat confused, I'll admit - the bit about the "hundreds-year long orbit" was presented in such a way as though it was supposed to be meaningful (complete with silhouette star shot), but honestly I can't really see how that's applicable. Perhaps as a clunky bit of foreshadowing (odds of Ayumi's power being related to starwatching are high), maybe.

My guess is it's more of a motif to set the tone of the show than a mechanism for the plot.

Astronomy is easily associated with wistfulness, isolation, and longing. Maeda loves anything that will make the viewer feel a connection like that on an emotional level. He used that kind of emotional connection a lot in his previous works. Tachibana at the piano in angel beats exploiting the soul of the piano, the empty otherworldly field in Clannad, the big wide lonesome sky in Air.

You're right though, It could be a key plot mechanism anyway. Either way I can't wait to see what he does with it.
Part of me hopes it's an established mechanism if only so that I can see if my theory is right, part of me hopes that it isn't truly established so that I can keep speculating my ass off.

How could human children have evolved the behavior to cry loudly all the time for no reason? Wouldn't this have attracted predators in the wild?

This might be a good question for /v/askscience

(Full disclosure: I'm a mod there if it matters)
The babies made good bait, so their families were better fed.
Most animals have that trait, so it must work.

Firstly, children (infants, more specifically) don't cry all of the time, they cry when they have discomfort or want attention. The factor that needs to be considered is whether an infant has a higher probability of dying due to predation, or due to other unmet needs (e.g. starvation, dehydration, exposure, etc.). It is possible that in the environment where crying evolved, it was the latter.

Now, the two things to bear in mind are 1. mutations are in individuals (i.e. they take time to propagate), and 2. evolution is selfish: it selects what is in the best interest of the individual, not the collective. Once crying was established (i.e. once the underlying genetics had proliferated), it would be disadvantageous for an individual infant to not cry: they would receive less attention than their peers, therefore be more likely to die; whereas, if even one infant in the group cries, any predators would be alerted.

It is possible that initially cries were very quiet, so had a high probability of alerting the mother with a much smaller probability of alerting predators. Once crying was established, however, infants competed for their mother's attention (this would be especially true for species that produce more than one baby at a time).

Also, studies suggest that an infant's cries induce a hormonal change in the mother; similar systems exist for silent communication via facial expression/emotion. It's possible that crying for attention was an evolution of emotional communication, which might make it even more immediately favourable selection-wise.

I'd imagine it wouldn't matter too much if it attracted predators. We're social animals, there's probably enough people around to scare away something that might scavenge a baby. There's probably a science or anthropology subverse that would know better though.
